headline: Google open-sources Long Horizon, revealing 5 design patterns for robust, long-running AI agents
summary: Long-horizon agents often fail silently, hiding problems over weeks. Google's new open-source harness, Long Horizon, addresses this with 5 crucial design patterns learned from real-world bugs.
details: Google Cloud has open-sourced Long Horizon, an agent harness built on its Agent Development Kit (ADK) under an Apache 2.0 license. This tool addresses a critical problem: "one-shot agents break and stop, but long-horizon agents break quietly, hide the problem, and keep running."

The project shares five key design patterns derived from real bugs encountered during weeks of internal testing. A recurring issue was that "nothing ever threw an error," indicating silent failures that required specific architectural solutions.

Initial attempts at prefix caching failed because dynamic memory injection at the prompt's start changed the prefix hash every turn. By moving dynamic memory to the end of the prompt, Google reduced prompt size from 70,000 to under 22,000 characters after the first turn.

Agents that learn need to extract and write memories. Doing this inline slowed responses significantly. The solution was write-behind caching, where responses are sent immediately, and memory extraction runs in the background.

Unlike stateless web requests, long-horizon agents are persistent processes that users return to. Standard deployments often wiped CLI tools installed by the agent, forcing reinstallation and progress reports.

When one agent's output becomes another's input, the parent agent needs to accurately determine success. Google found that a delegate agent's timeout, step limit, or normal completion all returned similar "envelope" structures, leading to hallucinated success reports.

Agents with shell access can access cloud metadata endpoints and credentials. A simple string match to block 169.254.169.254 was bypassed by curl http://2852039166/ (an integer representation of the same IP). The lesson: always normalize IP addresses before comparison.

These solutions primarily involve parsers, declarative rules, and auditable counters, not complex models. The final lesson emphasizes designing credentials assuming they will eventually be breached, injecting secrets, and running in a sandbox.

headline_marked: [[JarService/zhima Malware]] via Insecure Android Car Head Unit Update Paths
headline: JarService/zhima Malware via Insecure Android Car Head Unit Update Paths
summary: A supply chain attack distributes JarService/zhima Android malware through legitimate vehicle software update apps. It turns car head units into proxy nodes for ad fraud and external traffic relay.
details: A supply chain attack distributes multi-stage Android malware, JarService/zhima, through legitimate vehicle software update apps like TWCore. This malware transforms car head units into proxy nodes for ad fraud and external traffic relay.

Company vehicles, delivery vans, or shuttle cars using aftermarket or embedded Android head units running DoFun software are particularly vulnerable. These devices can become botnets, operating outside standard IT asset management and EDR visibility.

As a practical first step, organizations should inventory devices, firmware, and network connections. It is crucial to isolate vehicle and IoT terminals from internal corporate networks to prevent wider compromise.

Look for Indicators of Compromise (IOCs) such as unknown APKs via TWCore, C2 traffic with approximately 90-minute intervals, and unnatural relay traffic from vehicle network connections. If device logs are unavailable, network and asset data can serve as starting points for investigation.

Infections are often invisible, with the car screen appearing normal even when compromised. Users should not perform unauthorized resets or delete APKs; instead, report the model number and update status to management or the dealer.
